title: Bowing
hook: bowing in all schools, from a small bow to full prostration

segments.voice: Yesterday, the name chanted: Namo Amituofo, said step by step around a Chinese hall. Your line was walking the name. On day 2 you asked why Buddhists bow three times; today, the bow itself.

Soon after his awakening, an old discourse says, the Buddha sat alone and had a surprising thought. It is hard, he reflected, to live without someone to honor and respect. So he looked for someone wiser to bow to. In the whole world, he found no one. So he decided to honor the truth he had awakened to, the Dhamma itself. Even the awakened one, in this story, wanted something to honor.
screen: `JUST AFTER AWAKENING.` → `SOMEONE TO HONOR.` → `HE HONORS THE DHAMMA.`

segments.voice: First, the small bow. Across Buddhist schools, the simplest bow is palms together at the chest and a slight bend forward. Zen calls the folded hands gassho. It greets a teacher, a friend, a meal, a cushion before sitting on it. Second, the kneeling bow. In Theravada temples in places like Thailand and Sri Lanka, people lower forehead, forearms and knees to the floor, often three times: once for the Buddha, once for the Dhamma, once for the Sangha. Children learn it young; adults do it entering a shrine room, before a monk, or before sleep. Third, the full prostration. In Tibetan practice, people stretch the whole body flat on the ground, arms out ahead, then rise and do it again. Some do it daily in a shrine room; some pilgrims travel long roads this way, one body length at a time. Fourth, what a bow is for. Buddhist teachers say a bow is not groveling, and not worship of a statue. It lowers the self: the proudest part of you, the head, touches the same floor as the feet. In Zen, some teachers say that in a true bow there is no one bowing and nothing bowed to. In the Theravada telling, it honors what is worth honoring, as the Buddha himself chose to honor the Dhamma. Different schools, different heights, one movement: down, and back up.
screen: `PALMS TOGETHER: THE SMALL BOW.` · `KNEELING: BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA.` · `THE WHOLE BODY ON THE GROUND.` · `THE HEAD MEETS THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `DOWN, AND BACK UP.`

segments.voice: Bring your palms together at your chest and bow three times, as deep as your body allows, a nod, a bend at the waist, or kneeling to the floor, going slowly and noticing the lowering and the rising. If you're a Buddhist, you may bow to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha; if not, bow to whatever in your life you honor: a teacher, a parent, the day itself.
Bowing. Lowering the body in respect, from palms together and a slight nod to the whole body flat on the ground. School by school, the form changes. Today's word.
Your line: bow. The head and the feet, on the same floor. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Buddhists bow in their own ways: Zen practitioners bow with palms together, Theravada Buddhists kneel and touch the floor, often three times for the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, and Tibetan Buddhists practice full-length prostrations.

chat.says: Why do Buddhists bow down to a statue? Are they worshipping it?
options: Teachers say it isn't worship of a statue; it lowers the self and honors what's worth honoring.
It's just a polite habit from Asian cultures, with no meaning in the practice.
Only monks bow that low; lay Buddhists just stand and fold their hands.
chat.meaning: Buddhist teachers say a bow isn't groveling or worship of a statue: it lowers the self and honors what's worth honoring, as the Buddha honored the Dhamma.

notes: SN 6.2 (Garava Sutta) paraphrased: after awakening, the Buddha reflects that it is painful to dwell without reverence, finds no one superior, and resolves to honor the Dhamma. Confirm paraphrase and placement 'just after his awakening'.
The kneeling bow described (forehead, forearms and knees) without naming the five-point count; 'often three times' for Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha. Confirm.
Thailand and Sri Lanka named as examples of Theravada bowing practice; confirm.
Tibetan full-length prostrations and pilgrims who prostrate along long roads; confirm.
Zen sayings about bowing ('no one bowing and nothing bowed to') attributed to 'some teachers'; confirm acceptable as a paraphrase of a common Zen teaching.
